clue.text: Across the rough, but missing middle of green

indicators.note: something missing has been taken away, so a letter drops out of the phrase

parts.note: taken as written, run together

indicators.note: the middle of a word is its central letter, so only that one is taken

parts.note: the central letter of the five-letter word green

explanation.surface: A golfer's ball sails over the long grass but misses the centre of the putting green.
explanation.walkthrough: Dropping the E from THE ROUGH leaves THROUGH. The golf picture makes 'green' look like part of the course.
explanation.definitionFit: As a preposition, through can mean from one side to the other, the same as across.

clue.text: It's nonsense to monopolise Shaw play

indicators.note: to play with something is to toy with it, so these letters are moved about

parts.note: to hog something is to keep it all to yourself
the four letters of the playwright's name, rearranged

explanation.surface: A critic dismisses the idea of hogging all of George Bernard Shaw's plays as rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shaw play' looks like a drama by Shaw, but 'play' is the signal to rework the name.
explanation.definitionFit: Hogwash is informal slang for worthless talk, a direct synonym of nonsense.

indicators.note: without a top means the word loses its first letter, the top of a down entry

parts.note: a podium is a raised stand for a speaker or winner

explanation.surface: Someone is made to stand bare-chested as a public shaming.
explanation.walkthrough: PODIUM without its P leaves ODIUM.
explanation.definitionFit: Odium is general hatred or the shame that comes with it, so it can stand for disgrace.

indicators.note: done awfully means done badly, so the letters come out in a mangled order

parts.note: taken as written
P is the abbreviation for a penny
taken as written

explanation.surface: In a relay, Penny runs the final, anchor leg very badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Anchor leg' reads as the last stage of a relay race, but the anchor is the definition and the leg is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A grapnel is a small anchor with several hooked flukes, used to moor boats or grab objects.

indicators.note: containing means holding something inside, so one word sits within another

parts.note: a case is a box or container
a rat is a contemptible man, as is a cad

explanation.surface: Something tumbles down along with a box that has a rodent in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rat' is not the animal here but an untrustworthy man.
explanation.definitionFit: A cascade is a waterfall, especially one in stages, so the plural noun falls fits it.

parts.note: everyone is all of them
a flower here is something that flows, a river; the Ure is a river in Yorkshire

explanation.surface: Someone charms the whole room, carrying a flower.
explanation.walkthrough: In crosswords a 'flower' is often a river, a thing that flows; the Ure is a river in North Yorkshire.
explanation.definitionFit: Allure is attractive power or fascination, a synonym of charm as a noun.

clue.text: Fighter unable to take in order to hit

indicators.note: to take something in is to draw it inside, so one word wraps around others

parts.note: unable is can't, written without the apostrophe
the Order of Merit, a British honour, abbreviated OM
to bat is to hit, as with a cricket bat

explanation.surface: A boxer who cannot accept instructions to punch.
explanation.walkthrough: OM, the Order of Merit, is a British honour; 'order' here is not a command.
explanation.definitionFit: A combatant is anyone engaged in fighting, so it is a direct synonym of fighter.

clue.text: Stage hands either wing performing a Scottish dance

indicators.note: performers act out a routine, so these letters go through new moves

parts.note: all twenty letters, run together

explanation.surface: Backstage crew in both wings of a theatre join in a Scottish dance.
explanation.walkthrough: A long anagram: all twenty letters of the first four words rearrange into the dance.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dashing White Sergeant is a well-known Scottish country dance, done in sets of three at ceilidhs.

indicators.note: slightly means only to a small extent, so only part of the words is used

parts.note: the last letter of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: A fruit cake has a faint shine on it.
explanation.definitionFit: The ugli is a Jamaican citrus fruit, a cross between a grapefruit and a tangerine.

parts.note: surface reading: the usual procedure or layout
setter's reading: a standard is a flag, and the arrangement is how it is flown after someone dies

explanation.walkthrough: 'Standard' looks like an adjective meaning usual; it is a noun, a flag, lowered partway as a mark of mourning.
explanation.definitionFit: Flags are flown partway down the pole as a sign of respect when someone important has died.

clue.text: Meat extremely green, infested with slugs

indicators.note: a thing infested has pests inside it, so the outer letters hold another word
at the extremes means at the two ends, so only the outermost letters count

parts.note: first and last letters of green
slugs are bullets, and bullets are ammunition

explanation.surface: Some very unripe meat has been overrun by garden slugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slugs' are not the garden pests but bullets, hence ammunition.
explanation.definitionFit: Gammon is cured or smoked ham from the hind leg of a pig, a kind of meat.

indicators.note: exotic means strange and foreign, so the letters take an unfamiliar form

parts.note: taken as written, run together

explanation.surface: Someone announces that their partner is an unusual creature.
explanation.definitionFit: A terrapin is a small freshwater turtle, so it is an example of an animal.

clue.text: He passes student union, lacking form

indicators.note: a union brings things together and mixes them, so the letters combine in a new order

parts.note: taken as written, run together
L for learner, as on a learner driver's plate

explanation.surface: A man walks past the students' union looking unfit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Student union' reads as a single body, but 'student' gives L and 'union' signals mixing.
explanation.definitionFit: Shapeless describes something without definite shape, which is exactly lacking form.

parts.note: spin is public relations, abbreviated PR
sole means only, single, one
a ness is a headland, as in Loch Ness or Dungeness

explanation.surface: A shoe sole whirls round while someone bows their head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head bent' reads as a posture, but 'bent' alone is the definition, the noun meaning inclination.
explanation.definitionFit: A bent is a natural tendency or inclination, and proneness is a liability or tendency to something.

indicators.note: making an entry into something means going inside it

parts.note: bare means empty, as in bare shelves
g is the symbol for gravitational force, as in g-force

explanation.surface: Police break into a deserted boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Force entry' suggests barging in; the phrase splits so that 'Force' gives a letter and 'entry into' places it.
explanation.definitionFit: A barge is a long flat-bottomed boat used on canals and rivers to carry goods.

clue.text: Sharp turn — English opener dismissed, nothing included

indicators.note: an opener comes first, so only the first letter of the word is used

parts.note: the first letter of English

indicators.note: something included is put inside, so one letter goes within the others

parts.note: leg before wicket, a way a batsman is dismissed in cricket
zero, shaped like the letter O

explanation.surface: A cricket report: the English opening batsman is out for a duck, a sudden reversal of fortune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'English opener' reads as a batsman, but it is the first letter. LBW, leg before wicket, is a cricket dismissal where the ball hits the batter's leg.
explanation.definitionFit: An elbow is a sharp bend in a pipe, road or river, by comparison with the bent arm joint.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: ... green, the colour of Robin Hood's cloth
second meaning: the cathedral city in eastern England

explanation.walkthrough: 'Green city' sounds like an eco-friendly town; the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Lincoln green is a bright woodland colour of cloth once dyed in the English cathedral city of the same name.

indicators.note: in places one word inside the other

parts.note: to design something is to create it
a pit is a hole in the ground

explanation.surface: A flaw in a pattern causes a crackling noise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Design' is a verb here, not a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: To crepitate is to make a crackling sound, a rare verb used of joints and of lungs in medicine.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the player who throws the ball in baseball
second meaning: a large vessel for pouring liquid

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as someone hurling crockery; the two halves are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: In baseball the pitcher delivers the ball to the batter, and a pitcher is also a large pouring jug.

indicators.note: to retain is to hold on to, so one word keeps another inside it

parts.note: toil is hard work
short for referee, an umpire

explanation.surface: A plan for the workplace is drawn up to keep a match official on staff.
explanation.definitionFit: A trefoil is a three-lobed ornamental motif in architecture, so it is a kind of design.

clue.text: Shout of surprise repeated by mistake

parts.note: boo is shouted to startle someone
the same shout said a second time

explanation.surface: Someone yells to startle another person twice, by accident.
explanation.definitionFit: Boo-boo is informal, chiefly American, slang for a silly error or blunder.

clue.text: Social worker to run away with animal

parts.note: ants are social insects, and worker ants do the labour
to elope is to run off secretly to marry

explanation.surface: A social worker absconds with a creature in their care.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Social worker' is not a welfare professional but a social insect.
explanation.definitionFit: An antelope is a swift, horned grazing mammal of Africa and Asia, an example of an animal.

clue.text: Laugh at two birds lacking tail

indicators.note: without its tail, the second word loses its final letter

parts.note: first bird: the tit, a small songbird
second bird: the tern, a seabird

explanation.surface: Someone giggles at a pair of birds that have lost their tails.
explanation.walkthrough: TIT plus TERN without its N.
explanation.definitionFit: To titter is to give a short nervous or suppressed laugh, so it is a kind of laugh as a verb.

indicators.note: hear tells the solver to listen to how the words sound rather than how they are spelt

parts.note: as a command, exercise means have a go at physical education, PE

explanation.surface: An audience cheers a speaker who declares that physical exercise is worthless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hear, hear!' is the parliamentary cheer of agreement, but here it means listen to the sound.
explanation.definitionFit: Tripe is cow's stomach lining, and by extension slang for worthless nonsense, so it means rubbish.

clue.text: Sweetie (hot one) at top of yellow pack

parts.note: H for hot, as on a tap
taken as written

indicators.note: the top of a word is its first letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: the first letter of yellow
a pack is a group, a bunch

explanation.surface: A sweetheart, very attractive, stands out at the head of a pack in yellow jerseys.
explanation.definitionFit: Honeybunch is an affectionate term of endearment for a loved one, just like sweetie.

indicators.note: out of order means disarranged, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, run together

explanation.surface: A question about whether someone belongs to a society or has been expelled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In or out' looks like a membership question; 'club' is the golf kind.
explanation.definitionFit: An iron is a golf club with a metal head, numbered by loft, used for approach shots.

clue.text: Transpose nature's building blocks — thus oxygen, nitrogen etc

indicators.note: to transpose is to switch the order, here taking the letters back to front

parts.note: DNA is the molecule carrying genetic code, the blueprint of living things
thus means so, in that way
O is the chemical symbol for oxygen
N is the chemical symbol for nitrogen

explanation.surface: A chemistry lesson: rearranging life's basic components gives oxygen, nitrogen and other elements.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface lists elements, and 'etc' looks like the end of that list; it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Etc is short for et cetera, Latin for 'and the rest', which in English is the phrase and so on.

indicators.note: after places one piece behind the other in reading order

parts.note: Brie is a soft French cheese
to fly is to race along at speed

explanation.surface: Someone dashes off right after the cheese course.
explanation.definitionFit: Briefly means for a short time, so a thing done briefly is done quickly.
